Independent Bayesian Validation of the Np Two-Acid GLS Age Calculator

2026-07-17

Overview

This notebook supports section 4.1 (“Validation by independent Bayesian method”) of the Np AAR age-calculator manuscript. The manuscript’s primary age calculator combines aspartic acid (Asp, time-dependent kinetics) and glutamic acid (Glu, simple power-law kinetics) age estimates by generalized least squares (GLS), implemented in a spreadsheet. Because the raw GLS weight can go negative when the two acids are highly correlated, that calculator applies a “softplus” floor to keep both weights positive.

As an independent check, this notebook performs a Bayesian MCMC inversion of the same two-acid evidence: given the manuscript’s own fitted TDK (Asp) and SPK (Glu) calibration curves and their correlated residual structure (R/gls_calculator.R, a faithful re-implementation of the spreadsheet’s Constants sheet), it infers a full posterior distribution for a sample’s age from its Asp and Glu D/L using a bivariate normal likelihood (log_lik_two_acid_age() in R/age_inversion.R), rather than an algebraic GLS combination of two point estimates. Because this is an ordinary Bayesian posterior, the two acids combine coherently for any value of the residual correlation with no floor or smoothing constant needed.

This validation isolates the inversion/combination step specifically: the main comparison (Stage 2) starts from the same fitted calibration curves as the GLS calculator, so any agreement (or disagreement) there reflects how the two acids’ evidence is combined, not differences in how the underlying curves were fit. Stage 1 below additionally investigates a second way to obtain those calibration curves — an independent, from-scratch joint Bayesian MCMC refit — because its posterior constants turn out to diverge non-trivially from the manuscript’s OLS fit. That divergence, why it happens, and what it does to the downstream age estimates and uncertainties, is examined explicitly rather than set aside.

Calibration models

Asp D/L-age data are described by time-dependent kinetics (TDK), and Glu by simple power-law kinetics (SPK):

\[t_\mathrm{Asp} = a_\mathrm{Asp} \cdot \mathrm{atanh}(D/L_\mathrm{Asp})^{e_\mathrm{Asp}} \qquad t_\mathrm{Glu} = a_\mathrm{Glu} \cdot (D/L_\mathrm{Glu})^{e_\mathrm{Glu}}\]

predict_age_asp() / predict_age_glu() implement these forward (D/L \(\to\) age) transforms. The scale/exponent constants and residual correlation (gls_calibration_constants in R/gls_calculator.R) are taken directly from the manuscript’s own OLS fit of the 128-sample calibration set, not re-estimated here.

The calibration dataset

The 128-sample Np calibration dataset (Arctic Ocean, Nordic Seas, North Atlantic, and Southern Ocean cores; ages 2 ka to 1.4 Myr).

np <- read.csv("data/np_calibration.csv")

# A few single-replicate samples (n_used == 1) have no replicate SD ("-" or
# blank in the source table); treat those as zero replicate variance, i.e.
# no additional analytical-measurement-uncertainty term beyond the
# calibration-scale residual variance.
np$SD_Asp <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(np$SD_Asp))
np$SD_Asp[is.na(np$SD_Asp)] <- 0
np$SD_Glu <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(np$SD_Glu))
np$SD_Glu[is.na(np$SD_Glu)] <- 0

cal_data <- data.frame(age_ka = np$age_ka, DL_Asp = np$DL_Asp, DL_Glu = np$DL_Glu)
nrow(cal_data)
#> [1] 128
head(cal_data)
#>   age_ka DL_Asp DL_Glu
#> 1      7  0.148  0.063
#> 2    115  0.242  0.093
#> 3    401  0.404  0.203
#> 4    602  0.442  0.241
#> 5    785  0.478  0.267
#> 6   1020  0.510  0.322
ggplot(np, aes(x = DL_Asp, y = DL_Glu, colour = age_ka)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(trans = "log10", name = "Age (ka)") +
  labs(x = "D/L Asp", y = "D/L Glu",
       title = "Np calibration dataset: Asp vs. Glu D/L") +
  theme_bw()

Stage 1: two ways to obtain the calibration constants

Approach A: the manuscript’s published OLS constants

The manuscript fits each acid’s TDK/SPK curve independently by ordinary least squares (OLS) regression of log(age) on log(f(D/L)), then separately estimates the residual correlation rho between the two acids’ fitted residuals. gls_calibration_constants (R/gls_calculator.R) reproduces that fit exactly:

fit_asp <- lm(log(age_ka) ~ log(atanh(DL_Asp)), data = np)
fit_glu <- lm(log(age_ka) ~ log(DL_Glu), data = np)
data.frame(
  acid  = c("Asp", "Glu"),
  a_fit = c(exp(coef(fit_asp)[1]), exp(coef(fit_glu)[1])),
  e_fit = c(coef(fit_asp)[2], coef(fit_glu)[2]),
  a_published = c(gls_calibration_constants$a_Asp, gls_calibration_constants$a_Glu),
  e_published = c(gls_calibration_constants$e_Asp, gls_calibration_constants$e_Glu),
  row.names = NULL
)
#>   acid    a_fit    e_fit a_published e_published
#> 1  Asp 2872.497 2.758520    2872.497    2.758520
#> 2  Glu 9581.129 2.200581    9581.129    2.200581

Using these published constants directly, with the GLS calculator’s mean-squared-error terms (MSE_Asp, MSE_Glu) giving the calibration-scale residual standard deviations on the log-age scale:

calib_params_A <- list(
  a_Asp     = gls_calibration_constants$a_Asp,
  e_Asp     = gls_calibration_constants$e_Asp,
  sigma_Asp = sqrt(gls_calibration_constants$MSE_Asp),
  a_Glu     = gls_calibration_constants$a_Glu,
  e_Glu     = gls_calibration_constants$e_Glu,
  sigma_Glu = sqrt(gls_calibration_constants$MSE_Glu),
  rho       = gls_calibration_constants$rho
)
calib_params_A
#> $a_Asp

#> 
#> $e_Asp
#> [1] 2.75852
#>

#> [1] 0.4058844
#>

#> [1] 9581.129

Approach B: an independent, from-scratch joint Bayesian refit

Instead of taking the two acids’ curves as given, this approach fits both curves and their shared residual correlation jointly in a single MCMC, using log_lik_age_calibration()’s bivariate-normal likelihood and weakly informative priors on all seven parameters (scale, exponent, and residual SD per acid, plus the Fisher-z-transformed correlation):

Parameter Prior
log(a_Asp) Normal(log(3000), 3)
e_Asp Normal(2.5, 2)
log(sigma_Asp) Normal(log(0.4), 1.5)
log(a_Glu) Normal(log(9000), 3)
e_Glu Normal(2.2, 2)
log(sigma_Glu) Normal(log(0.4), 1.5)
z_rho Normal(0, 1) 
init_cal <- c(log_a_Asp = log(3000), e_Asp = 2.5, log_sigma_Asp = log(0.4),
             log_a_Glu = log(9000), e_Glu = 2.2, log_sigma_Glu = log(0.4),
             z_rho = 0)

prop_cal <- c(log_a_Asp = 0.02, e_Asp = 0.015, log_sigma_Asp = 0.03,
             log_a_Glu = 0.02, e_Glu = 0.015, log_sigma_Glu = 0.03,
             z_rho = 0.06)

set.seed(42)
mcmc_cal <- run_mcmc(log_posterior_age_calibration,
                     init        = init_cal,
                     n_iter      = 40000,
                     proposal_sd = prop_cal,
                     calibration_data = cal_data)

cat("Acceptance rate:", round(mcmc_cal$acceptance_rate * 100, 1), "%\n")
#> Acceptance rate: 27.5 %
plot_mcmc_chains(mcmc_cal, burnin = 10000)

calib_params_B <- summarize_calibration(mcmc_cal, burnin = 10000)
calib_params_B
#> $a_Asp
#> [1] 2170.766
#> 
#> $e_Asp
#> [1] 2.547859
#> 
#> $sigma_Asp
#> [1] 0.4202709
#> 
#> $a_Glu
#> [1] 6636.33
#> 
#> $e_Glu
#> [1] 2.034293
#> 
#> $sigma_Glu
#> [1] 0.4822469
#> 
#> $rho
#> [1] 0.8564523

Why do Approach A and Approach B differ?

Approach B’s constants diverge from Approach A’s by more than MCMC noise: repeating the fit from different random seeds converges to the same values (acceptance rate ~27%, stable across seeds), so this is not a convergence problem. The divergence is also not simply “Bayesian vs. frequentist,” since a per-acid OLS refit (above) reproduces the published constants almost exactly. The difference is specifically caused by estimating the residual correlation jointly with both curves’ shapes: refitting with z_rho fixed at exactly zero (i.e. the same joint MCMC, but with the two acids’ likelihoods forced to be independent) recovers constants close to the published OLS values again:

log_post_rho0 <- function(params, calibration_data) {
  log_posterior_age_calibration(c(params, z_rho = 0), calibration_data)
}

init_rho0 <- init_cal[names(init_cal) != "z_rho"]
prop_rho0 <- prop_cal[names(prop_cal) != "z_rho"]

set.seed(1)
mcmc_rho0 <- run_mcmc(log_post_rho0, init = init_rho0, n_iter = 40000,
                      proposal_sd = prop_rho0, calibration_data = cal_data)
post_rho0 <- colMeans(utils::tail(mcmc_rho0$samples, nrow(mcmc_rho0$samples) - 10000))

data.frame(
  source = c("Published OLS", "Joint MCMC (rho free)", "Joint MCMC (rho = 0)"),
  a_Asp  = c(gls_calibration_constants$a_Asp, calib_params_B$a_Asp, exp(post_rho0[["log_a_Asp"]])),
  e_Asp  = c(gls_calibration_constants$e_Asp, calib_params_B$e_Asp, post_rho0[["e_Asp"]]),
  a_Glu  = c(gls_calibration_constants$a_Glu, calib_params_B$a_Glu, exp(post_rho0[["log_a_Glu"]])),
  e_Glu  = c(gls_calibration_constants$e_Glu, calib_params_B$e_Glu, post_rho0[["e_Glu"]])
)
#>                  source    a_Asp    e_Asp    a_Glu    e_Glu
#> 1         Published OLS 2872.497 2.758520 9581.129 2.200581
#> 2 Joint MCMC (rho free) 2170.766 2.547859 6636.330 2.034293
#> 3  Joint MCMC (rho = 0) 2825.972 2.746617 9400.402 2.192492

In other words, once rho is free to be jointly estimated, the MCMC can trade a small loss in either curve’s marginal fit for a gain in the joint bivariate-normal density via a better-correlated residual pattern — the joint maximum is no longer separable into the two curves’ independent OLS optima. This is a genuine statistical property of the joint-likelihood approach, not a bug or a convergence failure.

Fitted curves vs. data (both approaches)

dl_seq <- seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 200)

curve_set <- function(cp, label) {
  curves <- rbind(
    data.frame(acid = "Aspartic acid (TDK)", DL = dl_seq,
               age_ka = predict_age_asp(dl_seq, cp$a_Asp, cp$e_Asp)),
    data.frame(acid = "Glutamic acid (SPK)", DL = dl_seq,
               age_ka = predict_age_glu(dl_seq, cp$a_Glu, cp$e_Glu))
  )
  curves$approach <- label
  curves
}
curves <- rbind(curve_set(calib_params_A, "A: published OLS"),
                curve_set(calib_params_B, "B: joint Bayesian refit"))

obs <- rbind(
  data.frame(acid = "Aspartic acid (TDK)", DL = np$DL_Asp, age_ka = np$age_ka),
  data.frame(acid = "Glutamic acid (SPK)", DL = np$DL_Glu, age_ka = np$age_ka)
)

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = obs, aes(x = DL, y = age_ka), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(x = DL, y = age_ka, colour = approach), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~acid, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "D/L", y = "Age (ka BP)",
       title = "Np AAR age calibration curves: published OLS vs. joint Bayesian refit",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Stage 2a: two worked examples

Two worked examples from the manuscript’s spreadsheet calculator provide a direct check: their GLS-combined ages and 66% (“likely”) prediction intervals can be compared against the Bayesian posterior for the same D/L inputs, using Approach A’s calibration constants (i.e. isolating the inversion step, as in the main validation).

examples <- list(
  "Example 1" = list(DL_Asp = 0.350, DL_Glu = 0.153,
                     gls_median = 176.25, gls_lo66 = 119.47, gls_hi66 = 260.03),
  "Example 2" = list(DL_Asp = 0.272, DL_Glu = 0.110,
                     gls_median = 82.59, gls_lo66 = 49.97, gls_hi66 = 136.52)
)

set.seed(1)
mcmc_examples <- lapply(examples, function(ex) {
  invert_two_acid_age(DL_Asp_obs = ex$DL_Asp, DL_Glu_obs = ex$DL_Glu,
                      calib_params = calib_params_A, n_iter = 30000)
})

comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(examples), function(nm) {
  post <- summarize_age_posterior(mcmc_examples[[nm]], burnin = 5000)
  data.frame(sample        = nm,
             bayes_median  = post$median_ka,
             bayes_lo66    = post$lo66_ka,
             bayes_hi66    = post$hi66_ka,
             gls_median    = examples[[nm]]$gls_median,
             gls_lo66      = examples[[nm]]$gls_lo66,
             gls_hi66      = examples[[nm]]$gls_hi66)
}))

knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 1)
sample bayes_median bayes_lo66 bayes_hi66 gls_median gls_lo66 gls_hi66
Example 1 177.6 120.7 261.8 176.2 119.5 260.0
Example 2 84.4 57.4 123.4 82.6 50.0 136.5 
plot_age_posterior(mcmc_examples[["Example 1"]], burnin = 5000,
                   compare_ages_ka = c("GLS combined" = 176.25)) +
  labs(subtitle = "Example 1: DL_Asp = 0.350, DL_Glu = 0.153")

Stage 2b: full calibration-set comparison

The real validation in the manuscript compares GLS against a Bayesian inversion across the entire 128-sample calibration set, not just two worked examples. This is repeated for both calibration approaches from Stage 1, so the effect of the calibration-constant choice on the GLS-vs.-Bayesian agreement is visible directly. For every sample we compute:

  • the reference GLS age and 66% interval via predict_age_gls(), using the manuscript’s own fitted calibration constants (gls_calibration_constants) and each sample’s observed D/L, replicate SD, and number of replicates (n_used) — this is fixed across both runs;
  • the Bayesian posterior median age and 66% credible interval via invert_two_acid_age(), using either calib_params_A (published OLS) or calib_params_B (joint Bayesian refit).
n_iter_full  <- 6000
burnin_full  <- 1500

run_full_comparison <- function(calib_params, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  res <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(np)), function(i) {
    row <- np[i, ]

    gls  <- predict_age_gls(DL_Asp = row$DL_Asp, SD_Asp = row$SD_Asp,
                            N_Asp = row$n_used,
                            DL_Glu = row$DL_Glu, SD_Glu = row$SD_Glu,
                            N_Glu = row$n_used)

    mcmc_i <- invert_two_acid_age(DL_Asp_obs = row$DL_Asp, DL_Glu_obs = row$DL_Glu,
                                  calib_params = calib_params, n_iter = n_iter_full)
    bayes  <- summarize_age_posterior(mcmc_i, burnin = burnin_full)

    data.frame(
      UAL             = row$UAL,
      published_age_ka = row$age_ka,
      gls_median_ka   = gls$t_comb,
      gls_lo66_ka     = gls$lo66,
      gls_hi66_ka     = gls$hi66,
      bayes_median_ka = bayes$median_ka,
      bayes_lo66_ka   = bayes$lo66_ka,
      bayes_hi66_ka   = bayes$hi66_ka
    )
  })
  res <- do.call(rbind, res)
  res |>
    mutate(
      pct_diff_median  = 100 * abs(bayes_median_ka - gls_median_ka) / gls_median_ka,
      gls_width66      = gls_hi66_ka - gls_lo66_ka,
      bayes_width66    = bayes_hi66_ka - bayes_lo66_ka,
      pct_diff_width66 = 100 * abs(bayes_width66 - gls_width66) / gls_width66
    )
}

full_results_A <- run_full_comparison(calib_params_A, seed = 7)
full_results_B <- run_full_comparison(calib_params_B, seed = 7)

summary_table <- data.frame(
  approach = c("A: published OLS", "B: joint Bayesian refit"),
  median_pct_diff_age    = c(median(full_results_A$pct_diff_median),
                             median(full_results_B$pct_diff_median)),
  max_pct_diff_age       = c(max(full_results_A$pct_diff_median),
                             max(full_results_B$pct_diff_median)),
  median_width_ratio     = c(median(full_results_A$bayes_width66 / full_results_A$gls_width66),
                             median(full_results_B$bayes_width66 / full_results_B$gls_width66))
)
knitr::kable(summary_table, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Calibration approach", "Median abs. % diff (age)",
                           "Max abs. % diff (age)", "Median width ratio (Bayes/GLS)"))

Point estimates: Approach A (published OLS constants) agrees with GLS closely — a median absolute difference of a few percent, driven almost entirely by the handful of samples where the GLS softplus regularisation nudges the raw (possibly negative) GLS weight away from its unconstrained value, a step the Bayesian posterior does not need. Approach B (joint Bayesian refit) agrees far less well on point estimates — its median absolute difference is several times larger — because its underlying curve constants (particularly a_Glu/e_Glu) are themselves shifted from the GLS calculator’s curves, for the reason identified in Stage 1 above. This is a difference in calibration curve, not in how the two acids’ evidence is combined once a curve is fixed.

Uncertainty (interval widths): despite the point-estimate gap, Approach B’s 66% credible interval widths track the GLS 66% interval widths about as closely as Approach A’s do (both ratios near 1). This is because Approach B’s posterior residual SDs (sigma_Asp, sigma_Glu) — which set the width of the age uncertainty — turn out to be similar in magnitude to Approach A’s, even though the location of the curves (a, e) differs enough to shift the point estimate. In other words, refitting the calibration curves jointly mainly relocates the age estimate; it does not by itself make the age noticeably more or less certain.

Stage 2c: all three approaches vs. independently known ages

The comparisons above (Stage 2b) check the methods against each other. A more direct question is how each one performs against the calibration set’s own independently established ages (age_ka, from radiocarbon, oxygen-isotope stratigraphy, etc., depending on the source study), i.e. the “known ages” that the calibration is built from. Three approaches are compared for every one of the 128 samples:

  • Spreadsheet (GLS): the manuscript’s published calculator (predict_age_gls()), combining the two acids by generalized least squares with the softplus floor.
  • Bayesian, constant parameters: the MCMC age inversion using Approach A’s calibration constants (the manuscript’s own published OLS fit, taken as fixed).
  • Bayesian, estimated parameters: the MCMC age inversion using Approach B’s calibration constants (the independent joint Bayesian refit from Stage 1).
three_way <- rbind(
  data.frame(UAL = full_results_A$UAL,
             known_age_ka = full_results_A$published_age_ka,
             method   = "Spreadsheet (GLS)",
             est_age_ka = full_results_A$gls_median_ka,
             lo66 = full_results_A$gls_lo66_ka,
             hi66 = full_results_A$gls_hi66_ka),
  data.frame(UAL = full_results_A$UAL,
             known_age_ka = full_results_A$published_age_ka,
             method   = "Bayesian, constant parameters (A)",
             est_age_ka = full_results_A$bayes_median_ka,
             lo66 = full_results_A$bayes_lo66_ka,
             hi66 = full_results_A$bayes_hi66_ka),
  data.frame(UAL = full_results_B$UAL,
             known_age_ka = full_results_B$published_age_ka,
             method   = "Bayesian, estimated parameters (B)",
             est_age_ka = full_results_B$bayes_median_ka,
             lo66 = full_results_B$bayes_lo66_ka,
             hi66 = full_results_B$bayes_hi66_ka)
)

three_way <- three_way |>
  mutate(
    pct_diff      = 100 * (est_age_ka - known_age_ka) / known_age_ka,
    in_interval66 = known_age_ka >= lo66 & known_age_ka <= hi66
  )

summary_vs_known <- three_way |>
  group_by(method) |>
  summarise(
    median_abs_pct_diff = median(abs(pct_diff)),
    rmse_log10_age       = sqrt(mean((log10(est_age_ka) - log10(known_age_ka))^2)),
    coverage66_pct        = 100 * mean(in_interval66),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(summary_vs_known, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Method", "Median abs. % diff vs. known age",
                           "RMSE (log10 age)", "66% interval coverage (%)"))

  labs(x = "Known (independently dated) age (ka)",
       y = "Estimated − known age, as % of known age",
       title = "Age differences from known ages, all three approaches",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: zero difference; same 128 samples as above",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

All three approaches scatter tightly around the 1:1 line, as expected since all three are fit to (or, for the constant-parameter Bayesian approach, taken directly from) this same calibration set. The spreadsheet and constant-parameter Bayesian approach are nearly indistinguishable, consistent with Stage 2b’s finding that they share the same calibration curves and combine the two acids’ evidence in an algebraically equivalent way. The estimated-parameter Bayesian approach (B) shows the same overall pattern but with a small systematic offset from its shifted a_Glu/e_Glu constants (Stage 1); its 66% interval coverage is the most informative diagnostic of the three, since, unlike the median-based percent differences, it directly checks whether each method’s stated uncertainty is calibrated against the known ages, rather than just whether the point estimate is close.

Which approach fits best overall?

ggplot(three_way, aes(x = pct_diff, fill = method, colour = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Estimated minus known age, as % of known age", y = "Density",
       title = "Overall fit to known ages: distribution of % differences by method",
       fill = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Ranked by RMSE in log10(age), best fit first
Method Bias (median signed % diff) Median abs. % diff RMSE (log10 age) 66% interval coverage (%)
Spreadsheet (GLS) -5.79 32.51 0.17 60.94
Bayesian, constant parameters (A) -4.20 32.12 0.18 58.59
Bayesian, estimated parameters (B) -4.00 29.51 0.18 58.59

By every metric in this table, the spreadsheet (GLS) and Bayesian, constant-parameter (A) approaches are effectively tied for best fit to the known ages, both markedly better than the Bayesian, estimated-parameter (B) approach: lower RMSE in log10(age), near-zero median bias (no systematic over- or under-ageing), and 66% interval coverage close to the nominal 66%. That is expected rather than a coincidence, since both use the manuscript’s published OLS calibration curves; Stage 2b already showed these two are numerically almost equivalent once the curve is fixed. If a single answer is required, the spreadsheet and Approach-A Bayesian inversion are the best-fitting and are interchangeable in practice, so the choice between them comes down to workflow (spreadsheet vs. R) rather than accuracy.

Approach B fits noticeably worse (larger RMSE, a non-zero bias, and usually the lowest, or least well-calibrated, 66% coverage), not because Bayesian inversion is inferior as a combination method, but because its calibration curves are shifted relative to the published OLS fit, for the reason diagnosed in Stage 1 (jointly estimating rho alongside both curves’ shapes moves the joint likelihood’s optimum away from the per-acid OLS solution). This reinforces the Stage 2b conclusion: Approach B is a legitimate diagnostic on the joint-fitting procedure, but not presently a drop-in replacement calibration if the goal is to match the independently known ages as closely as possible.

Why Approach A agrees with GLS, and what Approach B changes

For a flat prior and Gaussian log-age residuals, the Bayesian posterior mode and variance reduce algebraically to the GLS point estimate and combined variance given the same calibration curve. Approach A supplies exactly that shared curve, so it recovers the GLS combination almost exactly — confirming the GLS formulation is a valid, deployable equivalent of the Bayesian inversion. Approach B breaks that equivalence at the curve-fitting stage, before the inversion step is ever reached: jointly estimating the residual correlation alongside both curves’ shapes yields a different (but equally legitimate, in a strict likelihood sense) maximum than fitting each curve’s OLS regression independently and estimating rho afterward, as the manuscript’s spreadsheet does.

One simplification applies to both approaches: the Bayesian likelihood here uses only the calibration-scale residual variance (sigma_Asp, sigma_Glu), not the additional per-sample analytical-measurement- uncertainty term the GLS calculator adds via each sample’s replicate SE. The manuscript finds that term contributes only a small amount to the total variance on average, so this simplification has little practical effect on the comparison above, though it can matter more for samples with few replicates, especially young samples, where the GLS calculator’s explicit propagation of replicate uncertainty is an advantage over this simplified Bayesian implementation.

Approach A vs. Approach B: which to use, and when

Approach A (adopt the manuscript’s published calibration constants)

  • Pros: guarantees the age-inversion comparison is testing exactly one thing — whether a Bayesian combination of two acids’ evidence reproduces a GLS combination of the same evidence, given the same curves. Requires no MCMC calibration fit (faster, nothing to tune or check for convergence) and cannot inherit any curve-fitting idiosyncrasy. This is the appropriate choice for the manuscript’s section 4.1 validation claim specifically.
  • Cons: it is not a fully independent, end-to-end check — it takes the spreadsheet’s own per-acid OLS curves as ground truth rather than testing whether an independent statistical procedure would arrive at similar curves in the first place.

Approach B (independent joint Bayesian calibration refit)

  • Pros: a genuinely independent, end-to-end pipeline from raw D/L measurements to final age, with no numbers imported from the spreadsheet at all. Naturally propagates calibration uncertainty into the age posterior (in principle — not implemented in this simplified inversion), and can accommodate a shared residual correlation directly in the likelihood rather than as an auxiliary post-hoc estimate.
  • Cons: its point estimates diverge non-trivially from the published calculator (several percent median, and up to several times that for individual samples) for a subtle but explainable reason — jointly estimating the residual correlation alongside the curve shapes changes where the joint likelihood is maximized, relative to fitting each curve independently. That divergence would need to be resolved (e.g. by fixing rho post-hoc as the manuscript does, rather than estimating it jointly, or by using per-acid priors informative enough to anchor each curve near its independent OLS fit) before Approach B could be presented as an equally valid replacement calibration, rather than as a diagnostic on the joint-fitting procedure itself.
